G303.p: A general heading for stories about the Devil and his origins and actions.

G303.1.1.3.p: God turns an angel into the devil as punishment for trying to imitate God by creating the world.

G303.1.1.4.p: God creates the devil by striking a stone with his whip.

G303.1.2.2.p: God finds the devil hiding under a stone.

G303.1.6.p: Devils come into being from sinful priests.

G303.1.7.p: The Tuatha De Danann are regarded as demons or fallen angels.

G303.1.8.p: A male and a female devil are taken out of a corpse's belly.

G303.2.p: Various names given to the devil.

G303.2.2.p: The devil is called "the black one".

G303.2.3.p: The devil says his name is "Millearces", meaning he has a thousand ways to lead men into sin.

G303.10.4.2.p: Two devils come to a maiden who loves dancing and play music for her when she bathes.

G303.10.4.5.p: The devil dances with a maid and pushes his claws through her hands.

G303.10.7.p: The devil gives a person good luck in fishing and hunting.

G303.10.9.p: A calf that is entirely red, entirely black, or entirely white belongs to the devil.

G303.10.10.p: Lizards are regarded as the devil's offspring.

G303.10.11.p: The spurge-laurel plant is called the devil's bush.

G303.10.12.p: The devil owns the reeds that grow in marshes and water.

G303.10.13.p: Thistles and nettles are considered the devil's vegetables, planted or owned by him.

G303.10.14.p: The bagpipe is considered the devil's bellows, used to blow air into his fire or mischief.

G303.10.15.p: The devil has a hound, a dog that serves him.

G303.10.16.p: The devil has a servant who serves him.

G303.10.17.p: A bird acts as the devil's messenger.

G303.10.18.p: Angels who serve Satan, the fallen angels or demons who follow him.

G303.10.19.p: A well that belongs to the devil, often said to be a place of his haunting or power.

G303.11.p: The family relatives of the devil, such as his wife and children.

G303.11.1.1.p: The devil's son stays with his mother at night and takes his father's place.

G303.11.2.p: The devil has a son, a figure who belongs to the devil's family.

G303.11.2.1.p: The devil and his son quarrel and fight over how the earth should be divided between them.

G303.11.2.2.p: The devil's children and grandchildren carry out his work on his behalf.

G303.11.3.p: The devil has a mother, who is part of his family.

G303.11.3.1.p: The devil's mother rides on a goat.

G303.11.4.p: The devil has a grandmother, who is part of his family.

G303.11.4.1.p: The devil's grandmother keeps house for him. She is an old wrinkled woman with red eyes who also locks up hell.

G303.11.4.2.p: The devil's grandmother is bleaching linen or cloth whenever it snows.

G303.11.5.p: The devil has a daughter, who is part of his family.

G303.12.p: Various things that happen to the devil when he gets married.

G303.12.1.p: The devil courts an innkeeper's daughter, trying to win her as his wife.

G303.12.2.p: The devil marries a widow, who mistreats him.

G303.12.3.p: The devil marries an old unmarried woman who turns out to be a nagging, quarrelsome shrew and a stingy miser.

G303.12.4.p: The devil visits a woman and fathers children with her, starting a family.

G303.12.5.1.r: Despairing of ever finding herself a husband, the old maid exclaims: “I would marry even the devil, were he to marry me.” The devil takes her at her word. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3253, Legends Nos. 367ff.
G303.12.5.1.p: A girl is married off to a devil.

G303.12.5.2.p: The devil marries a girl who scorns him, but she escapes from him.

G303.12.5.3.p: The devil marries a girl whose rich mother will not let her wed the ordinary young men of the village, so the devil wins her hand.

G303.12.5.4.p: The devil courts a woman, but she learns who he really is in time to escape. A minister saves her by swallowing a candle after getting the devil to promise she will live as long as the candle burns.

G303.12.5.5.p: A girl who has been married to the devil escapes by bringing along the answers to his riddles. She uses them to get free of him.

G303.12.5.6.p: A girl whom the devil tries to woo is protected by a magic herb she wears, which keeps him from harming her.

G303.12.5.7.p: The devil takes the appearance of a girl's lover and sleeps with her. On her way home she meets the real lover, learns what happened, and dies.

G303.12.6.p: The devil appears in the form of a woman and courts a man.

G303.12.6.1.p: A man marries a she-devil after catching her as a succubus, a female demon that visits men. Years later her brothers invite the couple to a feast or wedding, and he receives gifts or her dowry.

G303.12.7.p: Sexual relations between the devil and human beings.

G303.12.7.1.p: Satan has sexual intercourse with Eve, the first woman.

G303.13.p: The devil is portrayed as foolish and easily outwitted.

G303.13.1.p: The devil cannot know or understand what people are thinking.

G303.13.2.p: The devil does things backward, such as starting to build a house from the top down.

G303.13.3.p: The devil tries to enclose too much land with a wall in one night and fails to finish.

G303.13.4.p: The devil tries to learn several trades and fails at all of them except making verses. He then idles in alehouses and sings songs.

G303.13.5.p: A simple-minded devil reveals how he can be driven away.

G303.14.1.p: The devil destroys by night what people build by day.

G303.14.2.p: The devil builds a bridge but leaves one stone out. No one dares to put in the final stone.

G303.15.p: Places where the devil is said to haunt.

G303.15.3.p: The devil haunts and troubles a particular house, making it a place of evil visitation.

G303.15.5.p: The ruins of a palace are haunted by Satan.

G303.15.6.p: Satan shows up at a feast from which poor people have been excluded.

G303.16.2.p: A person is protected from the devil's power through prayer.

G303.16.2.2.p: A person is saved from the devil by praying to the Virgin Mary.

G303.16.2.3.2.p: The devil flees when the pope blesses him.

G303.16.2.3.3.p: Devils vanish when a priest blesses bread.

G303.16.2.3.5.p: A seemingly pure stream is revealed by a blessing to be a devil's trap, and anyone who drinks from it dies.

G303.16.2.4.p: Devils are driven away by singing a hymn or psalm.

G303.16.2.5.p: A demon cannot harm a holy man or holy woman.

G303.16.3.2.p: A devil cannot bear a cross that has been made from the straps of a knapsack.

G303.16.3.3.p: Devils are put to flight by a cross made of leaves.

G303.16.5.p: Giving or performing a sacrament breaks the devil's power.

G303.16.5.2.p: A devil disappears when it is offered the host, the consecrated bread of communion.

G303.16.10.p: Angels save a person from the devil.

G303.16.19.p: Assorted other ways of escaping the devil or destroying his power.

G303.16.19.1.p: A man riding a horse is safe from the devil.

G303.16.19.2.p: If one spits on old discarded brooms, the devil will go along with one.

G303.16.19.13.p: The devil cannot follow a man across running water.

G303.16.19.14.p: The devil is driven off or injured by a silver bullet, which allows escape.

G303.16.19.15.p: The devil cannot enter a magic circle drawn to keep him out.

G303.16.19.16.p: The devil can be driven away by making a sacrifice.

G303.16.19.17.p: The devil vanishes because he becomes frightened.

G303.24.1.1.p: The devil shows the priest a long scroll listing the sins of the congregation.

G303.24.1.2.p: The devil writes people's faults on a goatskin.

G303.24.1.3.r: Finnish: FFC XXXIII 44 No. 59; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 427; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 126 No. 59; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
G303.24.1.3.p: The devil writes down the names of men on a hide in church; a woman laughs when she sees him doing it.

G303.24.1.4.p: The devil stands in the church doorway and writes down the names of his own people on a sheepskin.

G303.24.1.5.p: The devil in church fills his sack with obscene or immoral songs sung by the people.

G303.24.1.6.p: The devil writes down every idle word spoken in church; his parchment runs short, so he has to stretch it.

G303.24.1.7.p: The devil writes down the names of people who fall asleep during church services.

G303.24.1.7.1.p: The devil disturbs people in church, which is how he catches those who sleep there.

G303.24.1.7.2.p: The devil writes down the names of people who look backward during church services.

G303.24.1.8.p: The devil writes down the names of people who whisper during church services.

G303.24.1.9.p: The devil keeps two books: a small one for the sins of clergy, which confession erases, and a large one for the unconfessed sins of ordinary laypeople.

G303.24.2.r: (Cf. G303.16.5.) Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 49; Scala Celi 3a No. 5; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
G303.24.2.p: The devils in church worship the consecrated host, the bread used in the Mass.

G303.24.3.p: A devil who torments friars is made to repent when they sing the hymn "Te sanctum dominum."

G303.24.4.p: The devil destroys the church steeple.

G303.24.5.p: The devil, in the form of a dog, chews up Bibles, hymnbooks, and church account books inside the church.

G303.25.p: A catch-all group of assorted motifs about the devil, none of which fits a more specific heading.

G303.25.1.p: The devil is outwitted or defeated by a wolf, which is described as the most cunning foe the devil has.

G303.25.2.p: The devils are afraid of Saint Isaac, and flee or are held off by him.

G303.25.3.p: The devil prefers people who are careless or neglectful to any other kind of sin or weakness.

G303.25.4.p: The devil boils people alive in a large kettle.

G303.25.5.p: The devil's seat in hell is built from discarded fingernail clippings.

G303.25.5.1.p: Devils make small caps for themselves out of the clippings from people's fingernails.

G303.25.6.p: An old woman offers chickens to devils, but they refuse them, so she gives them to priests, who eat them.

G303.25.7.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 42 No. 51**; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 594ff., 796.
G303.25.7.p: A man shoots the devil with a gun loaded with silver.

G303.25.7.1.r: (Cf. D1385.4.) Lithuanian, Latvian, Livonian, Estonian, Ukrainian, Polish, Rumanian: *Balys Tautosakos Darbai VI 53—83.
G303.25.7.1.p: The devil is hit by a silver bullet.

G303.25.8.p: When a lawyer is buried, the devil follows the corpse, claiming it for hell.

G303.25.8.1.p: The devil follows the corpse of a procurator (a legal agent), as if claiming it.

G303.25.9.p: A ship carrying the devil on board sinks.

G303.25.10.p: A monk accuses the devil of taking something that does not belong to him, and the devil denies it.

G303.25.11.p: The devil takes the place of a woman who goes to spend the night with a priest.

G303.25.12.p: A farmer who trades horses with the devil gets the worse of the deal.

G303.25.13.p: The devil buys a woman's hair, paying with a silver coin that turns into a piece of wood, and she dies.

G303.25.14.p: A general heading for what devils eat and drink.

G303.25.14.1.p: Devils or night-spirits hold a feast of disgusting food and drink.

G303.25.14.2.p: The devil roasts a toad to eat.

G303.25.15.p: The devil owns certain animals, and these are listed as his own creatures in folk belief.

G303.25.15.1.p: A fish with no tail is said to be the devil's hog, a creature belonging to the devil.

G303.25.16.p: The devil has various objects or belongings that he owns or hands out.

G303.25.16.1.p: The devil gives a man a pipe, gun, or musical instrument, usually after the man has been blinded, in exchange for something.

G303.25.17.p: Devils hold dances and feasts of their own.

G303.25.17.1.r: (Cf. G303.7.1.2.2.) Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3276, Legends Nos. 441, 448, 454, 458ff., 466.
G303.25.17.1.p: A devil dressed as a gentleman invites a traveler to a feast or wedding that is really a devils' gathering.

G303.25.17.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index Nos. 3276f., Legends Nos. 425—438, 443f., 446f., 449—453, 460.
G303.25.17.2.p: A musician is hired to play music for devils or night-spirits while they dance.

G303.25.17.3.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3277, 3278, Legends Nos. 443—448, 450—459, 461f., 466.
G303.25.17.3.p: Devils prepare a wedding feast for a woman who has hanged herself.

G303.25.18.p: The devil can harm or touch a person's body but cannot take hold of the person's soul.

G303.25.19.p: A council or assembly of devils meets to discuss their affairs.

G304.r: (For troll as underground spirit or mountain spirit see F455. For troll-woman see G200—G299, Witches.) **E. Hartmann Die Trollvorstellungen im den Sagen und Märchen der skandinavischen Völker (Stuttgart, 1936); Norse: MacCulloch Eddic 285.
G304.p: A troll is treated as a kind of ogre.

G304.1.p: A troll (ogre) takes on a particular appearance or shape.

G304.1.1.p: A troll appears in the form of an animal.

G304.1.1.1.p: A troll takes the form of a fox.

G304.1.1.2.p: A troll takes the form of a hare.

G304.1.1.3.p: A troll takes the form of a goose.

G304.1.1.4.p: A troll takes the form of a crow.

G304.1.2.p: A troll appears in the form of an inanimate object.

G304.1.2.1.p: A troll appears as a cloud.

G304.1.2.2.p: A troll appears as a key.

G304.1.3.p: A troll that has many heads. It is a monstrous ogre-like creature whose appearance is described as having several heads.

G304.2.p: General traits and habits that set trolls apart from other beings. This heading groups the particular characteristics listed beneath it.

G304.2.1.p: A troll that can make fire. It produces flames from its body.

G304.2.1.1.p: A troll makes fire by lighting its fingers, so that they blaze like torches or lamps.

G304.2.1.2.p: A troll stretches its neck out so far that fire comes out of its lips.

G304.2.2.p: What trolls eat, or the food they are known for consuming.

G304.2.2.1.p: A troll's food makes people who eat it strong. Eating it gives men great strength.

G304.2.3.p: Magical or unusual abilities that a troll possesses.

G304.2.3.1.p: Locks open by themselves when a troll comes near, so the troll can enter without a key.

G304.2.4.p: Things that trolls strongly dislike or cannot bear.

G304.2.4.1.r: Fb “kirkeklokke” II 130b; Icelandic: Arnason Legends of Iceland (London, 1864) I 120, 124, Boberg; Swedish: Grimm Deutsche Mythologie II 798 n. 1; Finnish-Swedish: Landtman Finlands Svenska Folkdiktning VII 560.
G304.2.4.1.p: Trolls cannot stand the sound of church bells and are driven away or harmed by them.

G304.2.5.r: *Fb “sol” III 356a; Icelandic: Arnason Icelandic Legends (London, 1864) I 122, Boberg.
G304.2.5.p: A troll is destroyed when sunlight falls on it, either bursting apart or turning to stone.

G304.3.p: Things that belong to a troll, such as its home and animals.

G304.3.1.p: The troll's home is a castle or fortress.

G304.3.1.1.p: The door to the troll's castle is made of gold.

G304.3.2.p: Animals that belong to a troll.

G304.3.2.1.p: A troll drives a team of mice, harnessed together to pull its vehicle.

G304.3.2.2.p: A troll drives a carriage pulled by two male goats.

G304.3.2.3.p: A troll keeps a bear in its stable.

G304.3.2.4.p: A troll keeps hares in its stable among its other animals.

G305.p: An earl king, a supernatural ogre-like being of the wilds.

G306.p: A rainbow that acts as an ogre, a monstrous supernatural creature.

G307.p: A jinn, a supernatural spirit or demon that can influence human affairs.

G307.1.p: Explains the origin of jinn, where they come from.

G307.1.1.p: A jinn always appears out of a strong wind.

G307.2.p: The physical form or appearance a jinn takes.

G307.2.1.p: A jinn can take on any human shape it wants.

G307.2.2.p: A jinn is invisible to everyone except the people it chooses to show itself to.

G307.3.p: A jinn kills anyone who tries to live in a house the jinn has chosen as its home.

G307.4.p: A city overrun by jinn is abandoned by its people.

G308.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Persian: Carnoy 325; Jewish: Neuman.
G308.p: A sea monster, a creature living in the ocean.

G308.1.p: A hero or person fights a sea or lake monster.

G308.2.p: A monster that lives in water.

G308.3.p: Herds of sea monsters are seen swimming on the surface of the sea.

G308.4.p: A lake is made dangerous because a serpent, dragon or péist haunts it.

G308.5.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 191; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 13/346).
G308.5.p: A shark-like man-ogre who eats children who swim in the sea.

G308.6.p: A lake monster can lure its victims toward it.

G308.7.p: A clam shell tempts a man down into the sea to be eaten.

G308.8.p: Sea monsters that are two whales who were once human.

G308.9.p: A demon in the form of a giant octopus that lives in the sea and attacks people.

G310.p: A heading for ogres who are known mainly by the particular way they catch, kill, or trap their victims.

G311.r: Burr-woman. Ogre who jumps on one’s back and sticks there magically. *Chauvin VII 23 No. 373E; Fb “ryg” III 103ab; *Basset 1001 Contes I 190; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 126 No. 58; Greek: Grote I 7; Eskimo (Central): Boas RBAE VI 626; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 330 n. 191e; Africa (Luba): DeClerq Zs. f. Kolonialsprachen IV 226.
G311.p: An ogre appearing as an old man who lives at sea and preys on those who come near him.

G312.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 109, 291, 1113, II 950; Mono-Alu: Wheeler 14, 21.
G312.p: A giant or demon that eats human flesh.

G312.1.p: A pisaca, a flesh-eating demon that drinks blood, eats corpses, and wastes away the living.

G312.2.p: A female spirit living inside a rock who devours men and cattle.

G312.3.p: Man-eating spirits that dwell in trees.

G312.4.p: A man-eating ogre who fries his victims alive in a kettle of oil.

G312.5.p: Bhrat, fierce flesh-eating creatures that the Creator made in a fit of anger.

G312.6.p: An ogre who eats only the hearts of men.

G313.r: Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 131 n. 2, Fox 99; Jewish: Neuman.
G313.p: Procrustes, a monster who forces his captives to fit his bed: he cuts off the legs of tall men and stretches short ones.

G314.r: Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 124 n. 1, Fox 98.
G314.p: A pine bender, an ogre who kills people by letting a bent tree spring back on them.

G315.p: Cycnus, a monster who cuts off the heads of strangers to build a temple of skulls.

G316.p: A giant robber who attacks travelers with a club.

G317.p: An ogre who challenges people to wrestling matches and defeats them.

G321.r: Greek: Fox 99, Frazer Apollodorus II 129 n. 1; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 322 n. 163.
G321.p: A cliff ogre who kicks his victims over a cliff to their deaths.

G321.1.p: An ogre who pushes his victims into a hole.

G321.2.p: An ogress stationed at a spot along the road who takes the lives of those who pass.

G322.p: A monster who catches and devours men as if fishing for them.

G322.1.p: A giant who catches people by fishing, using his line to haul in ships and the men aboard.

G323.p: An ogre who hunts and traps game, is silent, and chases a trickster figure.

G327.p: Girls who swing their lovers out over a pit, cut the rope so they fall, and later eat them.

G328.r: *Fb “snog” III 436b; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 322 n. 161.
G328.p: Snakes that crawl into a living man's body and devour him from inside.

G328.1.p: A serpent lives inside a man's body and eats all the food he takes in, leaving him starving.

G331.p: An ogre who tilts a pot so that its victims are pulled into it.

G332.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Siberia: Holmberg Siberian 387; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 321 n. 158, (California): Gayton and Newman 72, cf. 95.
G332.p: A giant, sometimes a giant hall or cave, that sucks victims in.

G332.1.r: Cosquin Contes indiens 369 n. 1; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 80.
G332.1.p: An ogre sucks on a victim's finger until he has drunk all of the victim's blood.

G333.r: Scylla and Charybdis. Greek: Fox 137, 264; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 307 n. 113b.
G333.p: A path that runs between two monsters, so that anyone travelling it must pass between them.

G334.p: An ogre who holds human captives.

G334.1.p: An ogress holds twenty captive princesses in a cave.

G335.p: An ogre beheads a captive princess before leaving the palace, then brings her back to life when he returns.

G336.p: An ogre pulls victims down beneath the water.

G336.1.p: A demon pulls under the water anyone whose shadow falls on the surface of the water.

G341.p: Women who kill people with their elbows.

G341.1.r: S. A. Indian (Toba, Mataco, Shipaya, Warrau, Apinarje, Canella, Tukuna): Métraux MAFLS XL 74ff.
G341.1.p: An ogre with a sharpened leg used as a weapon.

G342.p: A demon with a pointed head, red hair, and a black face.

G345.p: A man with fire-making moccasins who sets fire to everything around him.

G345.1.p: An ogress who can make a cold oven blaze up simply by putting her foot into it.

G346.r: *Types 301, 550; Irish: *Cross, MacCulloch Celtic 126, 148f.; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 102; Finnish: Kalevala rune 46; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 12; Greek: Fox 56; India: *Thompson-Balys.
G346.p: A monster that destroys everything and lays waste to the land.

G346.0.1.p: A devastating monster that comes out of a hole in the ground in the evening to wreak havoc.

G346.1.r: Africa (Hausa): Mischlich 164ff No. 22, Frobenius Atlantis IX 277ff., 287ff. Nos. 74, 75.
G346.1.p: A devastating monster that makes a cat-like mewing sound.

G346.2.p: A devastating demon that kills and eats people.

G346.3.p: A monster that can live both on land and in water.

G346.4.p: An evil spirit that drinks up the water supply until it runs dry.

G347.p: An ogre named karumba who kills the hero using medicines or potions.

G350.p: Ogres that take the form of animals.

G351.p: A domestic farm animal that is really an ogre in disguise.

G351.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Tonga: Gifford 121, Beckwith Myth 342, 348.
G351.1.p: A dog that is really an ogre.

G351.2.r: Sucks blood. Kittredge Arthur and Garlagon 259 n. 2; Japanese: Mitford 245ff.
G351.2.p: A cat that is really an ogre.

G351.3.p: A fierce sow, a female pig, that is an ogre.

G351.4.p: An ogress who takes the form of a goat.

G351.5.p: An ogress who takes the form of a donkey.

G352.p: A wild animal that is really an ogre in disguise.

G352.1.r: Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 279, Snorra Edda Gylf. XII.
G352.1.p: A wolf that is really an ogre.

G352.2.p: A wild boar that is really an ogre.

G353.r: Tuamotu: Beckwith Myth 261, Stimson MS (z-G. 3/1229); Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 493.
G353.p: A bird that is really an ogre in disguise.

G353.1.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 78.
G353.1.p: A cannibal bird that is really an ogre.

G353.2.p: An eagle that is really an ogre.

G353.3.p: An ogre takes the form of a duck, a bird-shaped monster that preys on people.

G354.p: An ogre takes the form of a reptile, a cold-blooded creature such as a snake, crocodile or lizard.

G354.1.p: An ogre takes the form of a snake.

G354.1.1.p: A demon in the form of a serpent guards a forest in which a magic treasure tree grows.

G354.2.p: An ogre takes the form of a crocodile.

G354.3.p: An ogre takes the form of a lizard.

G360.p: General heading for ogres who are marked by monstrous bodily features rather than by their ordinary human shape.

G361.p: General heading for ogres with a monstrous head.

G361.1.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Africa (Fang): Einstein 149.

G361.1.1.1.p: A two-headed monster whose two horns each bear a human head.

G361.2.r: N. A. Indian (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 262, 291; S. A. Indian (Caviña, Tumupasa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 448, (Araucanian): Alexander Lat. Am. 329.
G361.2.p: An ogre who is essentially a huge head; the head comes off the body and pursues people or flies about causing harm.

G362.p: General heading for ogres with a monstrous nose.

G362.2.p: An ogre with a flat, upturned nose.

G363.p: An ogre whose mouth is grotesquely unnatural or monstrous in appearance.

G363.1.p: An ogre whose mouth shoots or contains flames.

G363.2.p: An ogre who has large tusks growing out of its mouth.

G363.3.p: An ogre whose teeth are made of diamonds.

G365.p: An ogre whose feet are unnatural or monstrous in form.

G365.1.r: Penzer IX 160; S. A. Indian (Araucanian): Alexander Lat. Am. 327.
G365.1.p: An ogre whose feet are turned backward.

G365.2.p: An ogress who can stretch out a leg or an arm to any length she wishes.

G366.p: An ogre whose body trunk is unnaturally or monstrously shaped.

G366.1.r: S. A. Indian (Fuegian): Alexander Lat. Am. 340.

G367.p: An ogre whose blood is unnatural or monstrous in some way.

G367.1.p: Five ogres whose blood is colored yellow, red, white, green, and black respectively.

G369.p: Assorted monstrous ogres who do not fit the other categories of monstrous features.

G369.1.r: Attack women. Hindu: Keith 98, Penzer X 277 s.v. “Rakshasas”; India: *Thompson-Balys.
G369.1.p: A rakshasa, a demonic man-eating ogre of Indian lore that can take many monstrous forms, such as a dog or ape shape, with red hair and eyes, a huge mouth, pointed ears, and sometimes multiple heads or horns. Rakshasas change shape and eat people and animals.

G369.1.1.p: A rakshasa is able to stretch its body to a distance of eighty miles.

G369.1.2.p: A rakshasa can be killed by a hero who has rakshasi blood flowing in his veins.

G369.1.3.p: A rakshasa eats many of the household animals every night.

G369.1.4.p: A rakshasa eats a horse, a dog, and a child.

G369.1.5.p: A man is tormented by a rakshasa who has taken the form of a beautiful woman.

G369.1.6.p: A rakshasa hidden inside a deer's head swallows men who come near.

G369.1.7.p: A rakshasa's mistress is found beheaded, lying in a pool of blood.

G369.2.p: A genie appears as a puff of smoke that takes shape as a creature with three wings, one of them growing on its back.

G369.3.p: An ogre who casts no shadow.

G369.4.p: An ogre who has the head and tail of a cat.

G369.5.p: A demon ogre reaches in through a chimney, door or similar opening with a long arm that ends in a demon's hand.

G369.6.p: An ogress who has only one breast.

G369.7.p: A demon with only one eye.

G370.p: A general heading for other kinds of ogres that do not fit the more specific categories.

G371.r: (Stone coats.) N. A. Indian (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 178, 330, 344, 438, 682.

G371.1.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 79.
G371.1.p: An ogre who is covered in or clothed in rock.

G372.r: Gaster Oldest Stories 47; Africa (Bushman): Bleek and Lloyd 193.
G372.p: Rain personified as an ogre who takes the form of a bull.

G375.p: Wonderful birds that are guarded by a monster.

G376.p: An ogre who appears disguised as a small boy.

G377.p: A monster stitched together from the parts of animal corpses and brought to life.

G400.p: A person is captured and falls under the power of an ogre.

G401.r: *Types 327, 327**; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 326 No. 1; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 48 No. 327E*, Espinosa Jr. No. 81; West Indies: Flowers 453.
G401.p: Children wander by chance into the house of an ogre.

G401.1.p: Two brothers are led to an ogre's home because an older brother made a wrong turn or error.

G402.p: A person chasing an animal is led to an ogre's house.

G402.1.p: A person chasing a bird is led to an ogre's house.

G402.2.p: A person chasing a mongoose is led to a witch's house.

G403.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 542b nn. 23—27; India: Thompson-Balys.
G403.p: An ogre takes the form of an animal in order to lure a victim and take them captive.

G405.r: Type 303; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
G405.p: A man out hunting falls into the power of an ogre or witch. The hunter is captured by a monstrous or magical being.

G406.p: A person who is lost or stranded in the wilderness falls into the power of an ogre. Getting lost leads directly to capture by a monster.

G410.r: India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 76 No. 1.
G410.p: A person is tricked or lured into the power of an ogre. Someone's betrayal or deception delivers them to a monster.

G411.p: A person helps an ogre and is then captured by it. The helper ends up trapped by the very creature they assisted.

G412.r: Mono-Alu-Fauru: Wheeler 44f.; Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 189, 311.
G412.p: Children are lured into an ogre's house by some enticement. They are drawn in and then trapped there.

G412.1.p: An ogre's house made of gingerbread or sweets attracts a child, who is then caught. This is the edible-house lure of the children-in-the-woods type.

G413.r: Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 64 No. 10; West Indies: Flowers 453.
G413.p: An ogre changes or disguises its voice so that it sounds like someone harmless, in order to lure a victim closer. The false voice is the bait.

G414.p: An ogress invites boys to come and live in her house. The boys accept the invitation and are then held by her.

G420.p: A person is seized and held by an ogre. This is the general heading for capture by such a creature.

G421.p: An ogre sets a trap that catches its victim. The victim is caught in the ogre's snare.

G422.p: An ogre locks a victim up and keeps them imprisoned. The captive is confined rather than immediately eaten.

G422.1.r: Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 62 No. 10, (Kaffir): Kidd 233 No. 4, (Yoruba): Ellis 261 No. 1.
G422.1.p: An ogre imprisons its victim inside a drum. The captive is shut up in the drum.

G423.p: A ball falls into water and this puts a person under the power of an ogre, witch, or water spirit. The fallen ball is the cause of the capture.

G424.p: A wedding party refuses to cross a bridge because they fear a water-demon lives beneath it. The fear keeps them from crossing.

G426.p: An ogre pulls a girl over a waterfall. The ogre drags her down the falls.

G440.p: An ogre carries off a person by force. The victim is abducted and taken away.

G441.r: *Type 327; Norwegian: Christiansen 43f. No. 327**; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen II 85; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 351 n. 268a, (California): Gayton and Newman 96; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 66 No. 10, (Kaffir): Theal 120, 134, (Zulu): Callaway 75.
G441.p: An ogre carries its victim away in a bag or basket. The captive is hauled off inside the container.

G442.p: A demon steals children. It is a child-stealing monster that snatches infants and young children away.

G442.1.p: An ogre takes a newborn baby and keeps it captive for seven years. The child is held away from its family during that time.

G442.2.p: A child is watched over all night to protect it from a child-stealing demon. Someone stays awake as a guard against the demon.

G450.p: A person is caught and taken under the control of an ogre, with no more specific circumstance given.

G451.p: A person follows a witch's fire or light and is thereby drawn into her power.

G452.p: A young person goes to work as a servant for an ogre.

G455.p: A person falls under an ogre's power because he is attracted to the ogre's daughter.

G461.p: A youth who has been promised to an ogre goes to live at the ogre's home.

G461.1.p: A boy in an ogre's house sees many human heads arranged in rows, and the heads smile and weep.

G462.p: A person is kept as a servant in an ogre's house.

G462.1.p: A hero works as the herder of goats belonging to a giant or ogre.

G463.p: An ogre correctly guesses a riddle or test and wins a princess as a result.

G464.p: An ogre oppresses and rules cruelly over the land of the fairies.

G465.p: An ogre gives a person tasks that cannot possibly be done.
